utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just make one small interruption and suggestion, not a criticism at all. My learned friend uses the phrase "about the night of the 20th" on page 47, line 22. Clearly what's being spoken about is the night, I think, of the 19th, morning of the 20th. Perhaps that should be amended, if that exactly is what's being said, so that when people look back at the evidence in the passage of time we know exactly what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, does Mr. Moore correctly understand your intended question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm thankful for this sort of cooperation from the OTP. Yes, that is what we're talking about, and I believe the witness has understood me. It might be an error in the transcript. We were talking about the night between the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991. Now we're talking about what happened on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have now explained this, there is one thing I want to know about this topic. We've heard testimony about this before this Tribunal. You headed for the door once the doctors and the medical staff had been told to the plaster room for a meeting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I passed that room, there were many medical workers in the room and outside the room assembled, which means that most of them had arrived there before I even started leaving the room that I was in in order to head for the hospital exit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you specify how long it took you to get from the x-ray room to the place where you were frisked or searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't take long. It's a corridor taking you straight to the auxiliary exit. It's as long as the building is wide. So it should be about 30 metres, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're familiar with the general layout, but what about the time line? Was it five minutes, ten, two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No way. Might have taken about two or three minutes. It's a very short stretch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Where were you, the men, separated from the women and children? Was it inside the building in the corridor, or outside the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the very exit. It was under that awning that was there, the covered area where an ambulance brings an injured person in order to protect that person from rain or snow. It was right there that this was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this was done by young soldiers, young JNA soldiers, regular soldiers, conscripts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the same place where the men were frisked or searched or was it outside in the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't done right there. Those of us, the men who were supposed to have left, having passed the exit and proceed towards Gunduliceva Street, we were lined up near the exit leading to Gunduliceva Street. There is a slight slope or incline there, which is closed off by a low wall along which we were made to line up, and that's where we were searched, but that was a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This last part of your answer suggests that the search took place a little later. From the point in time when you were separated from your wives and families to the point in time when you were frisked or searched, how long do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would find it very difficult to be specific, but it was a very short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing that I find to be substantial, when a person was searched, were they dispatched to the buses immediately, or did you remain there to stand in line before you were told to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed right there where we were and then an order would be given for us to go to the buses and that's when we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my understanding too. You said it was the lieutenant who gave the order, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is I knew that the lieutenant was in charge of monitoring the search, the frisking, and in charge of monitoring the process whereby people were being placed on those buses. I did not personally hear whether he was the one who issued the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I said I assumed based on your statement. I assume you have a copy in front of you, the one dated April 1996. If you could please open that statement, page 4 of the B/C/S. [In English] We are now on page 4 of English version of the statement. [Interpretation] Page 4, if you could please read the third passage, starting with the following sentence: "There was an officer there wearing JNA uniform." Read slowly for the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said page 4, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, third passage. "I heard that Major Sljivancanin," that's how it begins. And then: "There was an officer there." Can you see that portion? "There was an officer in a JNA uniform."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't seem to be able to find that. Sorry, you said the April statement? Which one is that supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the statement that you signed. That's the one I wish to discuss.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the one I was looking at was statement number 2, and that's why I was unable to find this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4, third passage, third sentence. "There was an officer" and so on, if you could please read that out to us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There was an officer in a JNA uniform. I heard later that he was a lieutenant who was in charge of searching people and taking us over to the buses." Yes, that's precisely what I said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one too, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This officer ordered us to get onto the buses. We didn't just go of our own accord. He was probably in charge and he was probably the one who ordered this." That's the overall meaning of this entire occurrence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question while ago was in order to refresh your memory and that's what I'm putting to you now by using this statement that you gave in 1996. I suppose your memory of events was much fresher back then. Do you remember that this man gave orders for you to go to the buses? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I didn't hear that. What I stated was that there was an officer there that probably saw this or heard this from other people, and the conclusion was that he was in charge of the search and of sending prisoners to the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your 1996 statement you didn't state that you heard this. You stated explicitly that this was something that you had seen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written like that, but you must know that I wasn't the one that was actually taking the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose that, too, is a kind of an answer. After the search, how long did you remain there, standing in the yard before you eventually got onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until about 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to be specific about this. Can you please tell us when the search began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 8.00 that we were called upon to leave the hospital and come out. Then we were separated and lined up and that took some time too. After we remained there standing waiting to see what would happen and then they started searching us, but it's very difficult to set a specific time line for all these events. It took until about 9.00, the whole thing was over at about 9.00, and -- well, the last group at least of which I was a part, we were placed onto that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're speaking about this topic, I would like to ask the registry to show the witness two photographs. I think it will be easier for all of us to deal with photographs rather than sketches or maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Witness, please, if you find it difficult to identify anything on these -- in these photographs, I will not be asking you to be make any further statements about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown a photograph from the 65 ter exhibit list. The number is 224 -- the photograph number is 0053-1260.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to wait a little because it will probably take a little time before the photograph can be shown. Can you see this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anything in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the hospital building; that's what I can see in the photograph. The one that we're talking about, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see in this photograph the exit that you took to -- in order to leave the hospital and outside which you were frisked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it very clearly, it's on the left-hand side of the photograph, you can see this short slope descending from the yard to the auxiliary exit at the back of the hospital leading into the surgery ward. You can even see this covered area, the awning that I referred to a while ago. It's a small roof, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fantastic. I think you will be even gladder to see the next photograph. But let's stick to this one for the time being. If you look at this photograph, can you see where the buses were parked on Gunduliceva Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can't see this particular portion of the road, but you can see very clearly the exit itself. There is a small reception room of sorts there. And you can see the hospital fence on the right-hand side towards the east, as it were. You can see another outbuilding that we called the gas building where the hospital's gas supply was stored that was used for the variety of purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will take advantage of your familiarity with this photograph in order for you to mark some things, so that all of us who are part of this trial are much clearer about what the photograph represents in the further course of the proceedings. Can you please use an arrow, or use the letter A to mark the spot where you were standing when you had just left the hospital, the place where you were frisked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could please put a letter A there. I can't see too clearly. And please draw a circle around it, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next photograph we'll try to be more precise. Does this mean that you were standing outside this wall at the entrance to the yard or were you still inside the tunnel, as it were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still inside the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please use an arrow to mark the direction in which you moved out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The auxiliary exit, you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, on your way to the buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So from where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark the spot where the buses were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no room here. But some of the buses were to the left of the exit, and some were parked to the right of the exit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please put a letter B there where you say the buses were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the photograph doesn't show the roadway. The buses where on the roadway. The witness has pointed out that the hospital fence can be seen and the roadway is below that. So we will have to imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that we all understand the layout now. We can assume that the street where the buses were parked is in the lower part of the photograph, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a pavement there, there's a meadow, and then the road. If I were to draw that in this photograph, I would have to draw it on -- over one of the roofs or the trees that are in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if we can see in this photograph the spot where you saw Martin Dosen lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was lying -- where you see the cars, it's just before this building that I refer to as the gas building. It's between the curved pavement and the road that he was lying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I assume that this is the spot right behind this tree in the lower right corner of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look from the hospital exit on the right-hand side -- you have the two roofs and you have the trees. It's right behind the second and the third one, the trees. I see that there are cars parked there. Sort of. Or perhaps sheltered from view by what appears to be the roof of a building across the way or something. It's both red and black and there's some sort of a triangle there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you place an arrow in that direction if you cannot see it and then mark that with a letter B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's no room. If I were to do that here where these cars are, that's not there because it -- they couldn't have been parked there because I don't know how long these cars have been there. But let's say that it was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark that spot with the letter B, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that outside of the hospital -- was he outside of the hospital compound or closer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that he was outside of the hospital compound between the pavement and the grassy area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell me one more thing while we're on this photograph. These five people who came out of the bus with their IDs and -- where were they standing and where did you have your dialogue with them? Can you mark the approximate spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about -- the place where this small gatehouse is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark that with the letter C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender this photograph with these markings into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the usher to show the witness another photograph from the same set. It's photograph 0053-1266.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise anything on this photograph? Can you tell what's being shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And it's much better and clearer than what we talked about so far. You can clearly see the exit here, and the ramp. And the exit where we were lined up and when -- where the place where we went out in the direction of Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how I understood it. Can you specifically show us the area on this photograph where you were searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pen is not working. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark that with the letter A, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark with the letter B the direction in which your wives went, where they were separated, can you show that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see just a part of the road because the building continues on and the road is to the right of the building. This part that you can see from the exit towards the road, I can mark that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you can mark that part with the letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this photograph into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to be looking at any more photographs. You don't have to look at the monitor anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you spent a day at the hospital, one day and one night. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know how many patients were at the hospital at that point in time? Were you told how many patients there were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that and nobody told me that. I also felt no need to find something like that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that straight from the room next to the X-ray room you went out and you found yourself outside of the hospital, and this trip took a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The trip only took a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not the last one because you entered the fourth bus and there were five more buses that were filled after you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please wait a little bit before beginning to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally were not able to see if all the men had left the hospital. You were not able to see them because you were not amongst the last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was amongst the last, because behind me, behind the people who were lined up, no more men left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see if any men did actually stay behind at the hospital. This is what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's something that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you cannot rule out the possibility that patients and other men remained behind at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Patients, absolutely, yes. As for men who were in some other category other than the ones who had been taken out, outside or told to go to the plaster room for certain announcements, well, other than those categories, I don't know if there were any other men who stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back for a moment to your statement, again very briefly, page 4 of the same statement. This part that you read out, "the officer ordered us to get into the buses," you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next sentence, well, I can read it or you can read it. Yes, please read it out loud and slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A certain number of the wounded," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence before that sentence, "There was not," that's how it begins?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There was no -- not any kind of system in order to get into the buses."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that to The Hague Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there and I accept that, but I probably didn't use the word "climbing" because to me the word "climbing" means to climb at a certain elevation. It doesn't fit into what I mean by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is not exactly what I would say I was shooting at in this question. The thing is: Do you remain by the statement that there were no criteria used as people were getting into the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were simply told, Please get into the buses. We were not told every fifth person or every seventh person or something, we were simply lined up, and then we started to move along, and then we entered the buses where there was space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understood your statement, but that does not coincide with what you said during your testimony in chief, where you said that you heard that patients were placed in the first three buses. So this does not accord with what you said? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group where I was mostly comprised civilians, but I heard, I have information that the patients and the wounded were taken out before I came out, and that they were placed in the first buses in the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you heard that exclusively patients and the wounded were placed into the first three buses, that there were no civilians of the same status as you in those buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the logical conclusion is that, because in my bus there were no patients or wounded persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you said is a product of your logical thinking, not a product of facts or information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's just logical based on what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, that this would be a good time for a break because after that I would move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a general question and then we'll go into more detail. From your testimony, both here and also from your statement, I concluded that you saw my client on two occasions. You first said that you saw Sljivancanin in the courtyard in front of the hospital, and that you saw him the second time when you spoke with him in front of the bus about the problem with your pass. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were staying at the barracks in Ovcara [as interpreted], you did not see him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to -- the transcript does not have it correctly. I said at the barracks and at Ovcara, and in the transcript it says at the barracks in Ovcara, but the witness and I understood each other well. What I said was that at the barracks and at Ovcara and also in the courtyard of the hospital as in the previous answer. You said that he was in the courtyard in that area. Did you say that he addressed you when you were standing in the courtyard in front of the hospital, in front of the exit for the emergency service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question by the Prosecution you said that you heard and you had the impression that he was a person in charge there, that he was issuing orders to the soldiers. That's what I understood from what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see insignia indicating that he was a major, or did you find out from the media later or based on some or information that he was a Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see insignia. I didn't even look for any, and perhaps it wasn't possible to see that from such a distance. But I heard from others that the gentleman was a major, and this was later confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You answered earlier that the lieutenant was present when you were interrogated and then also present when you were told that you were supposed to go to the buses. Did you personally see Sljivancanin issue orders to the lieutenant or to any other officer there? Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday and today you mentioned a person by the name of Martin Dosen; you described and also indicated on a photograph the place where he was lying. I'm interested in a few details about that. In your testimony you said -- and I assume that you saw that from the bus, you saw Martin Dosen from the bus, or am I wrong? You saw him from the bus when were you waiting to depart. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understood, you went to the buses at around 9.00, and you left the hospital at about 10.00, so you spent about an hour in the bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was roughly the length of time that we spent sitting in the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Dosen's wife, Ljubisa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall one more detail in relation to the time when you went out and also your conversation with my client about your papers. When did you see Dosen lying there? Before you went out, or once you got to the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before and after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he lying there when these five people left the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday during the examination-in-chief that his body was later found and identified at Ovcara. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that you heard that from someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps based on the information of those who perished at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in the courtyard or you while were on the bus, did you see anyone boarding an ambulance or a truck in that period while you were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the door of the emergency service until the time that you left the hospital area, all you saw were the five buses which were being boarded by the people from the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you about your alleged dialogue with my client about the problem with your medical ID. I'm going to be precise, and I am going to tell you exactly what you said. And this is in the transcript from yesterday. I'm going read that in English, that's how it was recorded in the transcript, and then you can tell me whether you still stand by what you said yesterday. It's page 15, line 3. [In English] "I got off the bus and I addressed Major Sljivancanin. I didn't know his name at the time. I just knew that he was a JNA major. He had looked at the IDs of those other five detainees. He said their passes or IDs were all right, and he said they should go back to the hospital." [Interpretation] That's what you said yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I conclude that you were present during his address or during his conversation with those people, then they left and the two of you stayed to discuss your problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were a little bit away from them, a few steps further from them, and the five of them spent a long time standing in that place where they came out, and then later they went to the hospital courtyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they go into the courtyard when you were still on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard Sljivancanin's conversation with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't tell us that yesterday. Can you please clarify for me. These five people came out, did you come out of the bus when he was still talking with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came out -- I came off the bus a little bit later than they did and then I was walking slowly towards the officer in question. I waited a little bit to the side until he finished the conversation with them. I didn't join their group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you assert that the officer in question was my client, Veselin Sljivancanin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session for a moment? I wanted to ask the witness about some people who are subject to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I deal with Mr. Vasic not evidentially, but in relation to clarification. Quite simply this: In his cross-examination of the witness, before we proceed, it was suggested at -- to the witness that there was a particular regiment or brigade that was at Ovcara. For my part it seemed to suggest, and from the transcripts I have got an "ATS 18th Brigade." Now, I don't know whether in actual fact that is correct, whether the interpreters have got it correctly or not. Could we perhaps just clarify whether it is right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I will only be too glad to clarify this matter for my learned friend. His quote is not correct. We are talking about the 80th Motorised Brigade based in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right away from the ATS 18th Brigade, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the clarification. Thank you very much for that. I have no re-examination in relation to Mr. Vasic's cross-examination. May I move on, then, to Ms. Tapuskovic, please, in relation to clarification, one matter. There was -- and then I have some questions. There was one matter that Ms. Tapuskovic did mention before going into private session. There was reference to names that were going to be named and then were not named. The only matter that I would wish to raise at this time, and I'm quite happy to go into private session, if needs be, is whether in actual fact it is going to be suggested later on in the trial certain names. And if that is the case, then this witness should have the opportunity in private session to either accept or deny or indeed say I do not know what those names were. My understanding was names were going to be put, but it depends really what is going to happen later on in the trial. Perhaps my learned friend could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the simple fact of the matter is during my cross-examination I just changed my mind and at one point no longer wished to ask the witness that question. I did say so, I believe, and I requested immediately to go back into open session. What I can say is that, as it happens, the question was later asked by my learned friend colleague Mr. Lukic, since his examination was more extensive on that subject. We are trying not to repeat ourselves, and we are trying to divide up certain areas in order to not take up too much time in cross-examination. So that's all there is to it. If Mr. Moore for a moment there believed that there was some sort of a mental reservation about my question on my part, that was certainly not the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would never consider there was any mental reservation by my learned friend Ms. Tapuskovic. I just wanted to make certain that we were dealing with the same topics. Thank you very much for that clarification. Re-examined by Mr. Moore:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I deal then, please, Witness, in respect of what you called the sixth bus that arrived at the JNA barracks. Do you remember being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You later on said to the Court that nobody knows what happened to them. It was not seen again. My question is this: Do you know where the sixth bus came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I just know that the sixth bus arrived later, after we got there, about half an hour later. Half an hour after the first five buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us about what I will call the attack on the bus by the individuals who were there, and you said nothing's known about the fate of the prisoners. Do you know any of the names of the individuals who were on that sixth bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to deal then, if I may, with one other topic. You told us about the hangar in Ovcara that you saw one young boy, you described him, I believe, as being 16 years of age, approximately, that he was taken outside and then he was returned to the hangar because his father was in the Croatian army. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that young boy who was taken back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the young man's name was Igor; that was his first name. I don't know his last name. And I didn't know the young man personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or have you been told what happened to that young man when he went back into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never been told. I don't know specifically what happened to him, but he ended up together with all the other prisoners who remained in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that young boy again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had he -- which district had he been living in prior to being taken to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come from Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-031 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I should assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. You will be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the questions for you so that your evidence is now at an end. The Chamber would express its thanks to you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given with -- by your evidence to the Tribunal. A court officer will now escort you out, and you are of course free to go back to your home and your ordinary affairs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we in a position to proceed, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour, yes. But there is one matter that I would seek the Court's assistance and guidance on. It really relates to the conduct of the trial and the speed of the trial. I mentioned at the very outset the possibility of using Rule 89 (F) as a method of producing evidence. Clearly the Defence are not fettered in any way of their ability to cross-examine. The Court indicated that initially perhaps there might have been a reluctance and to assist all parties to, as it were, get their bearings in relation to the case. The witnesses that we would be seeking to call in a sequence with the odd interruption because of certain difficulties that witnesses have. We have certainly one witness which will be a video link. Then we have other witnesses who will give evidence of Velepromet and Ovcara. They are, in our submission, important witnesses, but nevertheless there are areas that could be excluded. For my part I would respectfully ask the Court for guidance in relation to this, because I would submit that the time has now come to utilise 89 (F) in appropriate cases and to avoid repetition. The reason I mention it at this time is quite simply at the present moment the Prosecution have been on schedule with regard to their time estimates; indeed, I think we're slightly under on our time estimates. But we obviously have to inform witnesses who are being brought to court two or three weeks ahead, and at the present moment we are trying to bring three witnesses, sometimes four, depending on the nature of the evidence that is going to be given and the nature of the cross-examination. If we are going to use the 89 (F) procedure, and in my submission we should do so, then clearly I would be asking for more witnesses to be brought to the court complex, and I have to give those witnesses notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you identify the witnesses whom you would propose to follow 89 (F) procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I cannot do it immediately. It will take no more than five minutes to do so. But can I say straight away that virtually all the witnesses, and they break into two categories, we have one, what I would call military witnesses where -- and indeed experts which are under a different category, but there are witnesses, civilian witnesses, who deal with the Ovcara incident and the Velepromet incident which specifically relates to Count 1, obviously. And with regard to those witnesses, I would be inclined and submit that I could call virtually all of them under the 89 (F) procedure, as I submit it in no way is unfair to the Defence because they are able to cross-examine extensively and in no way are fettered in that cross-examination. It just stops repetition and court time is saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are proposing in the case of witnesses whom you have yet to specifically identify that you would call the witness, have them confirm the accuracy of their statement, enter the statement and then have the witness available for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just indicate what I was hoping to do? It would depend on the evidence given, shall we say, by Witness A. If Witness A gave evidence in chief, in part, nevertheless of course the statement we would submit would still go in as evidence and the Court would have that available to them. But it may be, for example, that there would be areas not cross-examined by my learned friends, so they would not contested areas, and they would not be contested areas for me. And therefore it would really depend on the evidence that would be given by the previous witnesses on how I adopted -- or the Prosecution adopted a course in dealing with the 89 (F) procedure. I couldn't say that every witness would just merely be, This is your statement, do you accept it as accurate, and I tender it as an exhibit. There may be witnesses where I would wish to particularise or specify or ask questions that have arisen as a direct consequence of cross-examination from my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you are contemplating that in addition to calling these witnesses and tendering their confirmed statement, there may be occasion for supplementary questions in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We would anticipate we would save at least one day a week if this procedure was adopted, and clearly fairness and justice has to be adhered to. That is the lodestar of any court. And we in our submission would -- do submit that that -- it doesn't affect that in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a position on this proposal? Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Above all, as far as Rule 89 (F) is concerned, the Defence believes that this has to be the exception rather than the rule applied when justice so requires. We are not entirely convinced that my learned friend has managed to persuade us that the issues of justice are at stake here. There may be other issues at stake here, but we do not believe that reasons of justice are involved. As for the groups of witnesses that he has referred to, if these are military persons, I suppose we are talking about members of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as I understand, nor any expert witnesses, merely for a number of factual witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I have simply misunderstood, but I believe there were two groups of witnesses being mentioned. A group of military witnesses, and another group of witnesses who will be testifying about Ovcara and Velepromet. That was my understanding. But these two groups were interrelated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It's the second group that Mr. Moore suggests would include many witnesses who might be dealt with under 89 (F), and I would understand that he says the interests of justice would justify this, including the speedier and more efficient use of trial time with no disadvantage being incurred to the Defence because you will have the normal opportunity to cross-examine. I think that's the effect of Mr. Moore's submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour. However, the way I see things, there are two problems arising. One in relation to our previous experience, the experience we have had so far, in relation to every witness, we regularly had statements dated 1995 and 1996, 10-year-old statements. Therefore, we kept receiving addenda for each and every of the witnesses provided by my learned friend. We are talking about recollections and memories that are 15 years old, in most cases. Another problem that I can see is if we look at what my learned friend has served on us as a witness list, those still remaining to be called, these witnesses were divided into groups, and some witnesses speak directly about the actions of the accused and their responsibility in the barracks and at Ovcara. As for Velepromet, this has no direct relation, but based on our previous experience here, based on the witnesses that we have heard and on the number of addenda provided by my learned friend, I do not think that merely tendering their statement into evidence would be an equitable solution because it will deny the Defence the right to hear the witnesses here, to hear what they have to say 15 years later, this being perhaps the second or even the third time they are examined, and this opens a whole lot of new possibilities for our cross-examination. Therefore, our position is that Rule 89 (F) should be used in a restrictive manner and only when the interests of justice are certain to be best served by applying that rule. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I believe that is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My position, Your Honour, is that when making a ruling on whether Rule 89 (F) should be applied in our proceedings in such a manner as my learned friend has just presented, I believe we must bear in mind Article 21 of the Statute and all the rights that any accused person must enjoy, including a fair and expeditious trial. If one decides to start applying Rule 89 (F), this might go into a degree of expeditiousness. However, I believe this would be at the expense of fairness. One thing we must bear in mind is that a total of 88 witnesses have been proposed, although on two separate occasions the OTP announced that they would maybe move to extend that list. We have 29 witnesses enjoying protective measures, the full set of protective measures, meaning closed session, voice distortion, facial distortion. We have 10 witnesses who will testify pursuant to 92 bis. What has been proposed, or suggested by my learned friend Mr. Moore for these witnesses to testify pursuant to Rule 89 (F), if I remember correctly, there must be about 30 of those witnesses, if my recollection of the list is accurate, which is about a third of the witness list in its entirety. I believe we have to keep all these things in mind before we decide whether it really serves the best interests of justice to apply Rule 89 (F). In my submission, Your Honour, this approach would be detrimental to the best interests of justice, and we would certainly achieve a more expeditious trial but not necessarily a fairer one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree and support the positions of my colleagues from the Defence entirely, but I would also like to add one thing. I noticed when you were deciding on Rule 92 bis and the introduction of certain statements that you strictly respected the sense of the 92 bis rule, and that is that these -- the parts relating directly to -- and you cited precisely in your decision what you considered to be direct or indirect, matters relating to the act -- actions of the accused. I think that in this treatment of Rule 89 (F) this is directly in contradiction to the sense of Rule 92 bis and that practically through a written statement if a witness is talking about acts and failures of the accused under 92 bis, and this is in the 89 (F) statements, it's something that a witness can only testify to in live testimony. Perhaps it would be much easier for the Prosecutor to decide which witnesses were repetitive and simply to give certain witnesses up, and that way we can save some time there, not to have witnesses repeat themselves, then we would save time in not repeating questions in cross-examinations for which we have already received answers and for which some conclusions had already been made. My proposal is that the witnesses who are called to testify before the Tribunal, especially keeping in mind the fact that a lot of these statements, and I think only these military statements were taken quite recently, but a large number of statements from the Croatian sides were actually taken in 1995, and you can see that there are differences in these statements. Now the Prosecutor would be in the position under our Rule 89 (F) to provide that statement and then also to give an annex to the statement and then avoid cross-examination. I believe that with this we cannot deal with the acts and -- actions and failures of the accused because that would be contrary to the sense of or intention of Rule 89 (F). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with the utmost respect, I fail to understand Ms. Tapuskovic's submissions in relation to Article 21. As far as I can understand, one of the criteria that's applied is the expeditious presentation of the evidence. Everything is a balancing act, and clearly what we say here is that the Defence are not fettered in any way in their cross-examination. That is the most important aspect of the -- ensuring a fair trial. The statements are taken in 1995. Of course I accept that, and I accept that addenda have been given. But the important point is that the Defence have not been disadvantaged by the method adopted by the Prosecution and would not be disadvantaged by the use of 89 (F) itself. With regard to my learned friend Mr. Lukic saying, well, you give up witnesses, with the utmost respect I will try, and have tried, although the Court may have not noticed it, to remove myself from repeating certain material that has been given earlier on. But we are now coming to the crux of the case, namely Velepromet, which relates specifically to Count 1 and generally to Counts 2 and 8, and then we move to the JNA barracks and clearly Ovcara. In our submission, it would be utterly wrong to give up witnesses that are relevant witnesses going to the elements of the offence that the Court has to determine merely for expedition. Fairness means fairness to all parties, not just the Defence. In our submission, we pose one very simple question: How do the Defence say that they are disadvantaged by the use of 89 (F)? Because we submit that they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, as I understood him, would put two matters at least. First, we are dealing with statements that typically are some 10 years old. And the experience to date in the trial suggests that witnesses, when they come here, recall matters differently from what has been recorded in their statement 10 years ago. And that it is, or it might well be of significance to assessing the credibility of that -- the witness and the difference to actually hear from the witness what is their present belief and understanding. What you propose would shortcut all of that and, as it were, we would hear their evidence essentially of 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour said there were two matters. Is that -- that's the first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second is the denial to the Defence of the opportunity to cross-examine on those differences once they have emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with the inconsistency point, what my learned friend Mr. Vasic is saying, we have a statement in 1995, we presumably have addenda, if there are any, and there have not been that many, or significantly, in relation to the witnesses, and then you have the statement given in evidence in chief. In our submission, consistency can be assessed quite easily by use of 89 (F) because the Defence would be entitled to compare the statement and the evidence. It does not in any way erode the ability to compare those two accounts. It may well be there is, I suppose, a third account, namely you have the 1995 statement, you have what I will call the addenda, the proofing where we give expansions or variations, which could be said to be inconsistent or clarification, depending whichever side you're on, and then thirdly, the evidence in chief. But equally the Court can look at the evidence that is being given and ask themselves this very simple question: To what extent have the witnesses deviated significantly from their statement and addenda when it came to their evidence in chief? In my submission, I can think of no example where a witness statement has been tendered as an exhibit so that the Court could compare the witness statement and the account given. And the Defence would be perfectly entitled to do so. So I would submit, in actual fact, the evidence that we have had tends to demonstrate that Mr. Vasic's concern has not got a sound basis. The inconsistency can still be demonstrated by way of comparison of the witness statement and the evidence in cross-examination. So I would submit that. Secondly, the second point is, and I'm -- I'm sorry, it seems to be suggesting that there would be an inability to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is missing, Mr. Moore, is the witness's actual present account of the witness's recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But if the witness himself says on oath, I have read this statement, I have created an addenda and signed that addenda as accurate, by adopting that particular statement and addenda he puts the stake in the ground in saying, This is my account and it remains the same. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Entirely correct as a proposition. I think you and I have seen courts enough to know that there is then often quite something different emerge in the course of the actual giving of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I certainly accept that. But can I equally submit that if there is actually something significantly different, is that not the very stake upon which the Defence use or use that stick to beat the Prosecution to demonstrate the proposition that in actual fact there is an inconsistency. It is, to some extent, a self-fulfilling prophecy, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I put another concern, Mr. Moore. The Chamber has been discussing the progress of the case and the course in particular of cross-examination. And it has seemed to the Chamber that quite a bit of time has been spent on small detail of the evidence of a witness, where somebody was standing, where somebody moved to, how many were there. Now, so far it has not often emerged what it is that that is directed to. We don't understand the point that is being made. It may be that it's merely exploring for credit. But we would have thought that the extent of this questioning suggests that there is a line of defence there, and that has not become terribly clear to us. Now, if we were to follow 89 (F) with all factual Prosecution witnesses about what is really the core of the case, which we haven't really got to yet, are you not likely to produce, as a consequence, a much more extensive and prolonged cross-examination as people for the Defence spend time trying to search out where there might be differences?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I respectfully submit in the nicest possible way, is Your Honour saying that two wrongs make a right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm saying to you that there are many factors at work here and they're not just simple. I personally have used an equivalent of 89 (F) for some years in civil proceedings. One of the consequences of that has been lengthier cross-examination because matters have not been gone through in chief, so Defence counsel, out of caution, whether the witness has a different view about something that may be of interest to the Defence case, go over that ground for themselves. Now, that has just been a normal and regular experience in an -- a court at superior level with very experienced counsel. So it's not clear-cut that if you use 89 (F) you save all the time that would be taken in evidence in chief. It spills over. It encourages the second problem that I have mentioned earlier. That is counsel just exploring in the hope that they may come across something of use and value rather than necessarily following a specific point, which it is seen is essential to pursue in the course of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I respectfully reply in the following way: I have little doubt with the experienced counsel that we have on the Defence side that they know their case, that the points that they are trying to establish, and that they will cross-examination -- there will be cross-examination as to that point. Of course it is entirely a matter for judicial discretion. Might I -- I'm not English and therefore I tend not to compromise. I tend to be of a nationality that tends to be rather dogmatic. But might I try and suggest a compromise in the sense that -- may I perhaps or the Court consider calling two or three witness 89 (F). I will particularise who they are and see whether in actual fact Your Honour's fears may manifest themselves or indeed we are able to save time. Time isn't the most crucial, important -- although I know that certain individuals within the administration may not look at it in that way. But nevertheless, time -- the undertakings that are given or the guide-lines that I've given, and I've spoken to my learned friends about when they believe this trial may conclude, vis-a-vis the Prosecution case, we may not be on time unless there is some flexibility in relation to the evidence which does not disadvantage the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This Chamber is guided by the fairness and the propriety of the trial, Mr. Moore. If it's going to take us until the end of 2007, it will. I'm confident it won't, but just to make it clear that we are not being driven by some artificial need to meet a time dead-line. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't trying to be rude in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to ensure that there is an efficient use of valuable court time. A use which focuses on the issues that matter in this case and is not spent loosely using time in the hope that somewhere in there there might be another point. You have not yet been in a position to indicate which witnesses you would propose this procedure for, nor have you sought to differentiate between those witnesses which are really at the forefront of your case, those who are most critical, and those who may be merely supportive of odd incidental matters. I would suggest that you might give attention to that, and that if the propositions you put were able to be focused on some supportive witnesses, and a few of them, and we can assess how that goes, and then see whether the process should continue or even be expanded that you might find the Chamber more at ease with your proposal. At the moment the notion just that all witnesses concerning what we're approaching, which is the core of the case, should simply come and tender statements, is a very sweeping proposition. So could we invite you, over the break, that is until next Tuesday, to look more closely at the particular witnesses you have in mind and see whether or not it would be possible at least as a trial to focus on a few who are less critical, and we could then consider that position, which I think is quite different from what you are now putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, running with that, two things: First, we would invite Defence counsel to look more closely at what is precisely their defence cases. The impression, and it may be quite wrong, but the impression we have often got is that questions are put merely in the hope that there may be something in there somewhere and precise details are sought in the hope that one or two of them may be confused or in error or something. This is a case where the fundamental issues are few and starkly clear. And we would hope that it will be possible to concentrate on those rather than spend a lot of time on small, minor detail that is not going to make much difference to anybody at the end of the day. And the last thing, and an important thing that the Chamber would want to emphasise, is that there does seem to have been a failure to effectively look at the issue of the agreement of facts. There seem to be a number of matters in this case which ought to be the subject of agreement which are not, and that can only mean then that the Prosecution has to press on with leading witnesses and spending time with a witness on matters which in the end will prove to be non-controversial, so we would urge all counsel to once again face up to the issue of agreement of facts. Now we say all of these things because it's in everybody's interests, above all each of the three accused, to get this long trial process over as quickly as possible. That is possible consistently with fairness. It's not going to do the accused, their families, and their friends good for this thing to drag on months longer than it need do. People want to get to the result and to get there as quickly as possible. So that we would urge counsel to look at the means available to them, to ensuring that we use our time efficiently and not waste it and just drag out the proceedings unnecessarily. Mr. Moore, we will look forward to hearing from you when we meet again on Tuesday. In the meantime, clearly we've run out of time, we cannot move to another witness today. We thank counsel for their assistance, and we will adjourn now until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.57 p.m.,
